entries.gloss: Aam, n. Etym: [D. aam, fr. LL. ama; cf. L. hama a water bucket, Gr.
Aar"on's rod`. Etym: [See Exodus vii. 9 and Numbers xvii. 8]
Ab-. Etym: [Latin prep., etymologically the same as E. of, off. See Of.]
Ab"a*cist, n. Etym: [LL abacista, fr. abacus.]
Ab*ac"ti*nal, a. Etym: [L. ab + E. actinal.] (Zoöl.)
A*bac"u*lus, n.; pl. Abaculi. Etym: [L., dim. of abacus.] (Arch.)
Ab"a*cus, n. E. pl. Abacuses ; L. pl. Abaci. Etym: [L. abacus, abax, Gr.
Ab"a*da, n. Etym: [Pg., the female rhinoceros.]
Ab*al`ien*a"tion, n. Etym: [L. abalienatio: cf. F. abalianation.]
A*ban"don, n. Etym: [F. abandon. fr. abandonner. See Abandon, v.]
A*ban"ga, n. Etym: [Name given by the negroes in the island of St. Thomas.]
A*base", v.t. [imp.&p.p. Abased; p.pr. & vb. n. Abasing.] Etym: [F. abaisser, LL. abassare, abbassare ; ad + bassare, fr. bassus low. See Base, a.]

A*bash", v.t. [imp. & p.p. Abashed; p.pr. & vb. n. Abashing.] Etym: [OE. abaissen, abaisshen, abashen, OF.esbahir, F. ébahir, to astonish, fr. L. ex + the interjection bah, expressing astonishment. In OE. somewhat confused with abase. Cf. Finish.]
A*ba"si*a, n. [NL.; Gr. - not + a step.] (Med.)
A*bate"ment, n. Etym: [OF. abatement, F. abattement.]
A`bat`toir", n.; pl. Abattoirs. Etym: [F., fr. abattre to beat down. See Abate.]
Ab"a*ture, n. Etym: [F. abatture, fr. abattre. See Abate.]
A`bat`voix", n. Etym: [F. abattre to beat down + voix voice.]
Ab*ax"i*al, Ab*ax"ile, a. Etym: [L. ab + axis axle.] (Bot.)
Abb, n. Etym: [AS. aweb, ab; pref. a- + web. See Web.]
Ab"ba, n. Etym: [Syriac abba father. See Abbot.]
Ab*ba"tial, a. Etym: [LL. abbatialis : cf. F. abbatial.]
Ab*bre"vi*ate, v.t. [imp. & p.p. Abbreviated; p.pr. & vb.n. Abbreviating.] Etym: [L. abbreviatus, p.p. of abbreviare; ad + breviare to shorten, fr. brevis short. See Abridge.]
Ab*bre`vi*a"tion, n. Etym: [LL. abbreviatio: cf. F. abbréviation.]
Ab*bre"vi*a`tor, n. Etym: [LL.: cf. F. abbréviateur.]
Ab*de"ri*an, a. Etym: [From Abdera, a town in Thrace, of which place Democritus, the Laughing Philosopher, was a native.]
Ab*de"rite, n. Etym: [L. Abderita, Abderites, fr. Gr. '
Ab"dest, n. Etym: [Per. abdast; ab water + dast hand.]
Ab"di*cant, a. Etym: [L. abdicans, p.pr. of abdicare.]
Ab"di*cate, v.t. [imp. & p.p. Abdicated; p.pr. & vb.n. Abdicating.] Etym: [L. abdicatus, p.p. of abdicare; ab + dicare to proclaim, akin to dicere to say. See Diction.]
Ab`di*ca"tion, n. Etym: [L. abdicatio: cf. F. abdication.]
Ab"di*tive, a. Etym: [L. abditivus, fr. abdere to hide.]
Ab*dom`i*na"les, n. pl. Etym: [NL., masc. pl.] (Zoöl.)
Ab*dom`i*na"li*a, n. pl. Etym: [NL., neut. pl.] (Zoöl.)
Ab*duce", v.t. [imp. & p.p. Abduced; p.pr. & vb.n. Abducing.] Etym: [L. abducere to lead away; ab + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Abduct.]
Ab*duct", v.t. [imp. & p.p. Abducted; p.pr. & vb.n. Abducting.] Etym: [L. abductus, p.p. of abducere. See Abduce.]
Ab*duc"tion, n. Etym: [L. abductio: cf. F. abduction.]
A*bear", v.t. Etym: [AS. aberan; pref. a- + beran to bear.]
A*bed", adv. Etym: [Pref. a- in, on + bed.]
Ab*err", v.i. Etym: [L. aberrare. See Aberrate.]
Ab*er"rant, a. Etym: [L. aberrans, -rantis, p.pr. of aberrare.]
Ab`er*ra"tion, n. Etym: [L. aberratio: cf. F. aberration. See Aberrate.]
Ab`e*run"cate, v.t. Etym: [L. aberuncare, for aberruncare. See Averruncate.]
A*bet", n. Etym: [OF. abet, fr. abeter.]
A*bey"ance, n. Etym: [OF. abeance expectation, longing; a (L. ad) + baer, beer, to gape, to look with open mouth, to expect, F. bayer, LL. badare to gape.]
Ab*hom`i*nal, a. Etym: [L. ab away from + homo, hominis, man.]
Ab*hor", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abhorred; p. pr. & vb. n. Abhorring.] Etym: [L. abhorrere; ab + horrere to bristle, shiver, shudder: cf. F. abhorrer. See Horrid.]
Ab*hor"rent, a. Etym: [L. abhorens, -rentis, p. pr. of abhorrere.]
A*bide", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abode, formerly Abid(#); p. pr. & vb. n. Abiding.] Etym: [AS. abidan; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + bidan to bide. See Bide.]
Ab"i*e*tene, n. Etym: [L. abies, abietis, a fir tree.]
Ab"i*gail, n. Etym: [The proper name used as an appellative.]
A*bime" or A*byme", n. Etym: [F. abîme. See Abysm.]
Ab*ir"ri*tate, v. t. Etym: [Pref. ab- + irritate.] (Med.)
Ab*ject", v. t. Etym: [From Abject, a.]
Ab*jec"tion, n. Etym: [F. abjection, L. abjectio.]
Ab*judge", v. t. Etym: [Pref. ab- + judge, v. Cf. Abjudicate.]
Ab"ju*gate, v. t. Etym: [L. abjugatus, p. p. of abjugare.]
Ab`ju*ra"tion, n. Etym: [L. abjuratio: cf. F. abjuration.]
Ab*jure", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abjured; p. pr. & vb. n. Abjuring.] Etym: [L. abjurare to deny upon oath; ab + jurare to swear, fr. jus, juris, right, law; cf. F. abjurer. See Jury.]
Ab*la"tion, n. Etym: [L. ablatio, fr. ablatus p. p. of auferre to carry away; ab + latus, p. p. of ferre carry: cf. F. ablation. See Tolerate.]
Ab"la*tive, a. Etym: [F. ablatif, ablative, L. ablativus fr. ablatus. See Ablation.]
Ab"laut, n. Etym: [Ger., off-sound; ab off + laut sound.] (Philol.)
A*blaze", adv. & a. Etym: [Pref. a- + blaze.]
A"ble, v. t. Etym: [See Able, a.] [Obs.]
Ab"li*gate, v. t. Etym: [L. ab + ligatus, p. p. of ligare to tie.]
Ab*lude", v. t. Etym: [L. abludere; ab + ludere to play.]
A*blush", adv. & a. Etym: [Pref. a- + blush.]
Ab*lu`tion, n. Etym: [L. ablutio, fr. abluere: cf. F. ablution. See Abluent.]
Ab*lu"vi*on, n. Etym: [LL. abluvio. See Abluent.]
Ab"ne*gate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abnegated; p. pr. & vb. n. Abnegating.] Etym: [L. abnegatus,p. p. of abnegare; ab + negare to deny. See Deny.]
Ab`ne*ga"tion, n. Etym: [L. abnegatio: cf. F. abnégation.]
Ab*nor"mi*ty, n.; pl. Abnormities. Etym: [LL. abnormitas. See Abnormous.]
Ab*nor"mous, a. Etym: [L. abnormis; ab + norma rule. See Normal.]
A*board", adv. Etym: [Pref. a- on, in + board.]
A*bol"ish, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abolished; p. pr. & vb. n. Abolishing.] Etym: [F. abolir, L. abolere, aboletum; ab + olere to grow. Cf. Finish.]
Ab"o*li"tion, n. Etym: [L. abolitio, fr. abolere: cf. F. abolition. See Abolish.]
A*bom"i*na*ble, a. Etym: [F. abominable. L. abominalis. See Abominate.]
A*bom"i*nate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abominated; p. pr. & vb. n. Abominating.] Etym: [L. abominatus, p. p. or abominari to deprecate as ominous, to abhor, to curse; ab + omen a foreboding. See Omen.]
A*bom`i*na"tion, n. Etym: [OE. abominacioun, -cion, F. abominatio. See Abominate.]
Ab*o"ral, a. Etym: [L. ab. + E. oral.] (Zoöl.)
A*bort", n. Etym: [L. abortus, fr. aboriri.]
A*bor"ti*cide, n. Etym: [L. abortus + caedere to kill. See Abort.] (Med.)
A*bor"tion, n. Etym: [L. abortio, fr. aboriri. See Abort.]
A*bor"tive, a. Etym: [L. abortivus, fr. aboriri. See Abort, v.]
A*bound", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Abounding.] Etym: [OE. abounden, F. abonder, fr. L. abundare to overflow, abound; ab + unda wave. Cf. Undulate.]
A*bout", prep. Etym: [OE. aboute, abouten, abuten; AS. abutan, onbutan; on + butan, which is from be by + utan outward, from ut out. See But, Out.]
A"bra, n. [Sp., a bay, valley, fissure.]
Ab`ra*ca*dab"ra, n. Etym: [L. Of unknown origin.]
Ab*rade", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abraded; p. pr. & vb. n. Abrading.] Etym: [L. abradere, abrasum, to scrape off; ab + radere to scrape. See Rase, Raze.]
A"bra*ham-man`(#) or A"bram-man`(#), n. Etym: [Possibly in allusion to the parable of the beggar Lazarus in Luke xvi. Murray (New Eng. Dict. ).]
A*braid", v. t. & i. Etym: [OE. abraiden, to awake, draw (a sword), AS. abredgan to shake, draw; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + bregdan to shake, throw. See Braid.]
A*bran`chi*a"ta, n. pl. Etym: [NL., from Gr. (Zoöl.)
Ab*rase", a. Etym: [L. abrasus, p. p. of abradere. See Abrade.]
Ab*ra"sion, n. Etym: [L. abrasio, fr. abradere. See Abrade.]
A*braum" or A*braum" salts, n. Etym: [Ger., fr. abräumen to remove.]
A*bray", v. Etym: [A false form from the preterit abraid, abrayde.]
Ab`re*ac"tion, n. [Pref. ab-+ reaction, after G. Abreagirung.] (Psychotherapy)
Ab`re*nounce", v. t. Etym: [L. abrenuntiare; ab + renuntiare. See Renounce.]
Ab`re*nun`ci*a"tion, n. Etym: [LL. abrenuntiatio. See Abrenounce.]
A`breu`voir", n. Etym: [F., a watering place.] (Masonry)
A*bridge", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abridged; p. pr. & vb. n. Abridging.] Etym: [OE. abregen, OF. abregier, F. abréger, fr. L. abbreviare; ad + brevis short. See Brief and cf. Abbreviate.]
A*bridg"ment, n. Etym: [OE. abregement. See Abridge.]
A*broach", v. t. Etym: [OE. abrochen, OF. abrochier. See Broach.]
Ab"ro*gate, a. Etym: [L. abrogatus, p. p.]
A*brook", v. t. Etym: [Pref. a- + brook, v.]
Ab*rup"tion, n. Etym: [L. abruptio, fr. abrumpere: cf. F. abruption.]
Ab*sces"sion, n. Etym: [L. abscessio a separation; fr. absedere. See Abscess.]
Ab*scind", v. t. Etym: [L. absindere; ab + scindere to rend, cut. See Schism.]
Ab*scis"sion, n. Etym: [L. abscissio. See Abscind.]
Ab*scond", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Absconded; p. pr. & vb. n. Absconding.] Etym: [L. abscondere to hide; ab, abs + condere to lay up; con + dare (only in comp.) to put. Cf. Do.]
Ab"sence, n. Etym: [F., fr. L. absentia. See Absent.]
Ab*sent", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Absented; p. pr. & vb. n. Absenting.] Etym: [Cf. F. absenter.]
Ab`sen*ta"ne*ous, a. Etym: [LL. absentaneus. See absent]
Ab"sinthe`, Ab"sinth`, n. Etym: [F. absinthe. See Absinthium.]
Ab*sol"u*to*ry, a. Etym: [L. absolutorius, fr. absolvere to absolve.]
Ab*solve" (#; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Absolved; p. pr. & vb. n. Absolving.] Etym: [L. absolvere to set free, to absolve; ab + solvere to loose. See Assoil, Solve.]
Ab*solv"ent, a. Etym: [L. absolvens, p. pr. of absolvere.]
Ab"so*nant, a. Etym: [L. ab + sonans, p. pr. of sonare to sound.]
Ab"so*nous, a. Etym: [L. absonus; ab + sonus sound.]
Ab*sorb", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Absorbed; p. pr. & vb. n. Absorbing.] Etym: [L. absorbere; ab + sorbere to suck in, akin to Gr. absorber.]
Ab*sorb"ent, a. Etym: [L. absorbens, p. pr. of absorbere.]
Ab*sorpt`, a. Etym: [L. absorptus, p. p.]
Ab*sorp"tion, n. Etym: [L. absorptio, fr. absorbere. See Absorb.]

Ab*stain", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abstained; p. pr. & vb. n. Abstaining.] Etym: [OE. absteynen, abstenen, OF. astenir, abstenir, F. abstenir, fr. L. abstinere, abstentum, v. t. & v. i., to keep from; ab, abs + tenere to hold. See Tenable.]
Ab*ster"gent, a. Etym: [L. abstergens, p. pr. of abstergere.]
Ab*ster"sion, n. Etym: [F. abstersion. See Absterge.]
Ab*ster"sive, a. Etym: [Cf. F. abstersif. See Absterge.]
Ab"sti*nence, n. Etym: [F. abstinence, L. abstinentia, fr. abstinere. See Abstain.]
Ab*stract", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abstracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Abstracting.] Etym: [See Abstract, a.]
Ab*strac"tion, n. Etym: [Cf. F. abstraction. See Abstract, a.]
Ab*strude", v. t. Etym: [L. abstrudere. See Abstruse.]
Ab*struse", a. Etym: [L. abstrusus, p. p. of abstrudere to thrust away, conceal; ab, abs + trudere to thrust; cf. F. abstrus. See Threat.]
Ab*stru"sion, n. Etym: [L. abstrusio. See Abstruse.]
Ab*sume", v. t. Etym: [L. absumere, absumptum; ab + sumere to take.]
Ab*sump"tion (#; 215), n. Etym: [L. absumptio. See Absume.]
A*bu"na, n. Etym: [Eth. and Ar., our father.]
A*buse", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abused; p. pr. & vb. n. Abusing.] Etym: [F. abuser; L. abusus, p. p. of abuti to abuse, misuse; ab + uti to use. See Use.]
A*bu"sive, a. Etym: [Cf. F. abusif, fr. L. abusivus.]

A*but", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abutted; p. pr. & vb. n. Abutting.] Etym: [OF. abouter, aboter; cf. F. aboutir, and also abuter; a (L. ad) + OF. boter, buter, to push: cf. F. bout end, and but end, purpose.]
A*bysm", n. Etym: [OF. abisme; F. abime, LL. abyssimus, a superl. of L. abyssus; Gr. Abyss.]
A*byss", n. Etym: [L. abyssus a bottomless gulf, fr. Gr.
Ac`a*deme", n. Etym: [L. academia. See Academy.]
Ac`a*de*mi"cian (#; 277), n. Etym: [F. académicien. See Academy.]
A*cad"e*my, n.; pl. Academies. Etym: [F. académie, L. academia. Cf. Academe.]
Ac"a*leph, Ac`a*le"phan n.; pl. Acalephs, Acalephans. Etym: [See Acalephæ.] (Zoöl.)
Ac`a*le"phæ, n. pl. Etym: [NL., from Gr.
A*can"thine, a. Etym: [L. acanthinus, Gr. Acanthus.]
A*can`tho*ceph"a*la, n. pl. Etym: [NL., from Gr. (Zoöl.)
Ac`an*thop"ter*i, n. pl. Etym: [NL., from Gr. (Zoöl.)
Ac`an*thop`ter*yg"i*i, n. pl. Etym: [NL., from Gr. (Zoöl.)
A*can"thus, n.; pl. E. Acanthuses, L. Acanthi. Etym: [L., from Gr. Acantha.]
A*cap"su*lar, a. Etym: [Pref. a- not + capsular.] (Bot.)
Ac`a*ri"na, n. pl. Etym: [NL., from Gr. (Zoöl.)
Ac"a*roid, a. Etym: [NL., acarus a mite + -oid.] (Zoöl.)
Ac`ar*pel"lous, a. Etym: [Pref. a- not + carpel.] (Bot.)
Ac"a*rus, n.; pl. Acari. Etym: [NL., from Gr. (Zoöl.)
A*cau"date, a. Etym: [Pref. a- not + caudate.]
Ac`au*les"cent, a. Etym: [Pref. a- not + caulescent.] (Bot.)
A*cau"line, a. Etym: [Pref. a- not + cauline.] (Bot.)
A*cau"lose, A*cau"lous, a. Etym: [Gr. caulis stalk. See Cole.] (Bot.)
Ac*ca"di*an, a. Etym: [From the city Accad. See Gen. x. 10.]
Ac*cede", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Acceded; p. pr. & vb. n. Acceding.] Etym: [L. accedere to approach, accede; ad + cedere to move, yield: cf. F. accédere. See Cede.]
Ac*cel"er*ate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accelerated; p. pr. & vb. n. Accelerating.] Etym: [L. acceleratus, p. p. of accelerare; ad + celerare to hasten; celer quick. See Celerity.]
Ac*cel`er*a"tion, n. Etym: [L. acceleratio: cf. F. accélération.]
Ac*cen"sor, n. Etym: [LL., from p. p. accensus. See Accend.] (R. C. Ch.)
Ac*cent", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accented; p. pr. & vb. n. Accenting.] Etym: [OF. accenter, F. accentuer.]
Ac*cen"tor, n. Etym: [L. ad. + cantor singer, canere to sing.]
Ac*cen"tu*ate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accentuated; p. pr. & vb. n. Accentuating.] Etym: [LL. accentuatus, p. p. of accentuare, fr. L. accentus: cf. F. accentuer.]
Ac*cen`tu*a"tion, n. Etym: [LL. accentuatio: cf. F. accentuation.]
Ac*cept", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accepted; p. pr. & vb. n. Accepting.] Etym: [F. accepter, L. acceptare, freq. of accipere; ad + capere to take; akin to E. heave.]
Ac*cess" (#; 277), n. Etym: [F. accès, L. accessus, fr. accedere. See Accede.]
Ac*ces"sion, n. Etym: [L. accessio, fr. accedere: cf. F. accession. See Accede.]
Ac*ces"so*ry (#; 277), a. Etym: [L. accessorius. See Access, and cf. Accessary.]
Ac*ciac`ca*tu"ra, n. Etym: [It., from acciaccare to crush.] (Mus.)
Ac`ci*den"tal, a. Etym: [Cf. F. accidentel, earlier accidental.]
Ac"ci*die, n. Etym: [OF. accide, accidie, LL. accidia, acedia, fr. Gr.
Ac*cip"i*ent, n. Etym: [L. accipiens, p. pr. of accipere. See Accept.]
Ac*cip"i*ter, n.; pl. E. Accipiters. L. Accipitres. Etym: [L., hawk.]
Ac*claim", v. t. Etym: [L. acclamare; ad + clamare to cry out. See Claim, Clamor.] [R.]
Ac`cla*ma"tion, n. Etym: [L. acclamatio: cf. F. acclamation.]
Ac*cli`ma*ta"tion, n. Etym: [Cf. F. acclimation. See Acclimate.]
Ac*cli"mate (#; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acclimated; p. pr. & vb. n. Acclimating.] Etym: [F. acclimater; à (l. ad) + climat climate. See Climate.]
Ac*cli"ma*tize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acclimatized; p. pr. & vb. n. Acclimatizing.]
Ac*cli"vous (#; 277), a. Etym: [L. acclivis and acclivus.]
Ac*coast", v. t. & i. Etym: [See Accost, Coast.]
Ac*com*bi*na"tion, n. Etym: [L. ad + E. combination.]

Ac*com"mo*date, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accommodated; p. pr. & vb. n. Accommodating.] Etym: [L. accommodatus, p. p. of accommodare; ad + commodare to make fit, help; con- + modus measure, proportion. See Mode.]
Ac*com"pa*ny, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accompanied; p. pr. & vb. n. Accompanying] Etym: [OF. aacompaignier, F. accompagner, to associate with, fr. OF. compaign, compain, companion. See Company.]
Ac*com"ple*tive, a. Etym: [L. ad + complere, completum, to fill up.]
Ac*com"plice, n. Etym: [Ac- (perh. for the article a or for L. ad) + E. complice. See Complice.]
Ac*com"plish, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accomplished, p. pr. & vb. n. Accomplishing.] Etym: [OE. acomplissen, OF. accomplir, F. accomplir; L. ad + complere to fill up, complete. See Complete, Finish.]
Ac*com"plish*ment, n. Etym: [F. accomplissement, fr. accomplir.]

Ac*cord", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accorded; p. pr. & vb. n. According.] Etym: [OE. acorden, accorden, OF. acorder, F. accorder, fr. LL. accordare; L. ad + cor, cordis, heart. Cf. Concord, Discord, and see Heart.]
Ac*cord"a*ble, a. Etym: [OF. acordable, F. accordable.]
Ac*cord"ant, a. Etym: [OF. acordant, F. accordant.]
Ac*cord"ment, n. Etym: [OF. acordement. See Accord, v.]
Ac*cost" (#; 115), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accosted; p. pr. & vb. n. Accosting.] Etym: [F. accoster, LL. accostare to bring side by side; L. ad + costa rib, side. See Coast, and cf. Accoast.]
Ac*cou*cheur", n. Etym: [F., fr. accoucher. See Accouchement.]
Ac*cou*cheuse", n. Etym: [F.., fem. of accoucher.]
Ac*count"ant, n. Etym: [Cf. F. accomptant, OF. acontant, p. pr.]
Ac*cou"ple, v. t. Etym: [OF. acopler, F. accoupler. See Couple.]
Ac*cour"age, v. t. Etym: [OF. acoragier; à (L. ad) + corage. See Courage.]
Ac*court", v. t. Etym: [Ac-, for L. ad. See Court.]
Ac*cou"ter*ments, Ac*cou"tre*ments, n. pl. Etym: [F. accoutrement, earlier also accoustrement, earlier also accoustrement. See Accouter.]

Bip"e*dal, a. Etym: [L. bipedalis: cf. F. bipédal. See Biped, n.]
Bi`pin*na"ri*a, n. Etym: [NL., fr. L. bis twice + pinna feather.] (Zoöl.)
Bi*po"lar, a. Etym: [Pref. bi- + polar. Cf. Dipolar.]
Bi*pu"pil*late, a. Etym: [Pref. bi- + pupil (of the eye).] (Zoöl.)
Bi*quin"tile, n. Etym: [Pref. bi- + quintile: cf. F. biquintile.] (Astron.)
Bi*ra"di*ate, Bi*ra"di*a`ted, a. Etym: [Pref. bi- + radiate.]

Birch, n.; pl. Birches. Etym: [OE. birche, birk, AS. birce, beorc; akin to Icel. björk, Sw. björk, Dan. birk, D. berk, OHG. piricha, MHG. birche, birke, G. birke, Russ. bereza, Pol. brzoza, Serv. breza, Skr. bh. sq. root254. Cf. 1st Birk.]
Bird"lime`, n. Etym: [Bird + lime viscous substance.]
Bi"reme, n. Etym: [L. biremis; bis twice + remus oar: cf. F. birème.]
Bi*ros`trate, Bi*ros"tra*ted, a. Etym: [Pref. bi- + rostrate.]
Birr, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Birred; p. pr. & vb. n. Birring.] Etym: [Cf. OE. bur, bir, wind, storm wind, fr. Icel. byrr wind. Perh. imitative.]
Bir"rus, n. Etym: [LL., fr. L. birrus a kind of cloak. See Berretta.]
Birt, n. Etym: [OE. byrte; cf. F. bertonneau. Cf. Bret, Burt.] (Zoöl.)
Bis, adv. Etym: [L. bis twice, for duis, fr. root of duo two. See Two, and cf. Bi-.]
Bis"co*tin, n. Etym: [F. biscotin. See Biscuit.]
Bis"cuit, n. Etym: [F. biscuit (cf. It. biscotto, Sp. bizcocho, Pg. biscouto), fr. L. bis twice + coctus, p. p. of coquere to cook, bake. See Cook, and cf. Bisque a kind of porcelain.]
Bi*sect", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bisected; p. pr. & vb. n. Bisecting.] Etym: [L. bis twice + secare, sectum, to cut.]
Bi*se"ri*al, Bi*se"ri*ate, a. Etym: [Pref. bi- + serial, seriate.]
Bi*se"tose, Bi*se"tous, a. Etym: [Pref. bi- + setose, setous.]
Bi*sex"ous, a. Etym: [L. bis twice + sexus sex: cf. F. bissexe.]
Bish"op, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bishoped; p. pr. & vb. n. Bishoping.]
Bis*mil"lah, interj. Etym: [Arabic, in the name of God!]
Bis"muth, n. Etym: [Ger. bismuth, wismuth: cf. F. bismuth.] (Chem.)
Bisque, n. Etym: [A corruption of biscuit.]
Bis"son, a. Etym: [OE. bisen, bisne, AS. bisen, prob. for bis; bi by + s clear, akin to seón to see; clear when near, hence short-sighted. See See.]
Bis"ter, Bis"tre, n. Etym: [F. bistre a color made of soot; of unknown origin. Cf., however, LG. biester frowning, dark, ugly.] (Paint.)
Bis"tort, n. Etym: [L. bis + tortus, p. p. of torquere to twist: cf. F. bistorte.] (Bot.)
Bis"tou*ry, n.; pl. Bistouries. Etym: [F. bistouri.]
Bi*sul"cous, a. Etym: [L. bisulcus; bis twice + sulcus furrow.]
Bit, n. Etym: [OE. bitt, bite, AS. bite, bite, fr. bitan to bite. See Bite, n. & v., and cf. Bit a morsel.]
Bi*take", v. t. Etym: [See Betake, Betaught.]
Bit"ter*ness, n. Etym: [AS. biternys; biter better + -nys = -ness.]
Bit"tock, n. Etym: [See Bit a morsel.]
Bitts, n. pl. Etym: [Cf. F. bitte, Icel. biti, a beam. (Naut.)
Bi*tu"men, n. Etym: [L. bitumen: cf. F. bitume. Cf. Béton.]
Bi*tu"mi*nate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bituminated; p. pr. & vb. n. Bituminating.] Etym: [L. bituminatus, p. p. of bituminare to bituminate. See Bitumen.]
Bi*tu"mi*nize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bituminized (; p. pr. & vb. n. Bituminizing.] Etym: [Cf. F. bituminiser.]
Bi*tu"mi*nous, a. Etym: [L. bituminosus: cf. F. bitumineux.]
Biv"a*lent, a. Etym: [L. bis twice + valens, p. pr. See Valence.] (Chem.)
Bi"valve, n. Etym: [F. bivalve; bi- (L. bis) + valve valve.]
Biv"i*ous, a. Etym: [L. bivius; bis twice + via way.]
Biv"i*um, n. Etym: [L., a place with two ways. See Bivious.] (Zoöl.)
Blab, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blabbed (p. pr. & vb. n. Blabbing.] Etym: [Cf. OE. blaberen, or Dan. blabbre, G. plappern, Gael. blabaran a stammerer; prob. of imitative origin. Cf. also Blubber, v.]
Black*bur"ni*an war"bler. Etym: [Named from Mrs. Blackburn, an English lady.] (Zoöl.)
Black"en, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blackened; p. pr. & vb. n. Blackening.] Etym: [See Black, a., and cf. Black, v. t. ]
Black"-eyed` Su"san. (Bot.) (a) The coneflower, or yellow daisy (Rudbeckia hirta). (b) The bladder ketmie.
Black Hand. [A trans. of Sp. mano negra.]
Black"mail`, n. Etym: [Black + mail a piece of money.]
Blad"der, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bladdered; p. pr. & vb. n. Bladdering.]
Blan"card, n. Etym: [F., fr. blanc white.]
Blanch, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blanched; p. pr. & vb. n. Blanching.] Etym: [OE. blanchen, blaunchen, F. blanchir, fr. blanc white. See Blank, a.]
Blan"chard lathe. [After Thomas Blanchard, American inventor.] (Mach.)
Bland, a. Etym: [L. blandus, of unknown origin.]
Blan*da"tion, n. Etym: [Cf. L. blanditia, blandities, fr. blandus. See Bland.]
Blan"dise, v. i. Etym: [Same word as Blandish.]
Blan"dish, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blandished; p. pr. & vb. n. Blandishing.] Etym: [OE. blaundisen, F. blandir, fr. L. blandiri, fr. blandus mild, flattering.]
Blan"ket, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blanketed; p. pr. & vb. n. Blanketing.]
Blan*quette", n. Etym: [F. blanquette, from blanc white.] (Cookery)

Blare, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blared; p. pr. & vb. n. Blaring.] Etym: [OE. blaren, bloren, to cry, woop; cf. G. plärren to bleat, D. blaren to bleat, cry, weep. Prob. an imitative word, but cf. also E. blast. Cf. Blore.]
Blar"ney, n. Etym: [Blarney, a village and castle near Cork.]
Bla*sé", a. Etym: [F., p. p. of blaser.]
Blas*pheme", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blasphemed; p. pr. & vb. n. Blaspheming.] Etym: [OE. blasfem, L. blasphemare, fr. Gr. : cf. F. blasphémer. See Blame, v.]
Blas"phe*my, n. Etym: [L. blasphemia, Gr. : cf. OF. blasphemie.]
Blast, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blasted; p. pr. & vb. n. Blasting.]
Blas*te"ma, n.; pl. Blastemata. Etym: [Gr. bud, sprout.] (Biol.)
Blas"tide, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout, fr. to grow.] (Biol.)
Blas`to*car"pous, a. Etym: [Gr. sprout, germ + fruit.] (Bot.)
Blas"to*cyst, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout + E. cyst.] (Biol.)
Blas"to*derm, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout + E. derm.] (Biol.)
Blas`to*gen"e*sis, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout + E. genesis.] (Biol.)
Blas*toid"e*a, n. pl. Etym: [NL., fr. Gr. sprout + -oid.] (Zoöl.)
Blas"to*phore, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout + to bear.] (Biol.)
Blas"to*pore, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout + E. pore.] (Biol.)
Blas"to*sphere, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout + E. sphere.] (Biol.)
Blas"to*style, n. Etym: [Gr. sprout, bud + a pillar.] (Zoöl.)
Blas"tu*la, n. Etym: [NL., dim. of Gr. a sprout.] (Biol.)
Blath"er (blath"er), v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Blathered; p. pr. & vb. n. Blathering.] [Written also blether.] [Icel. blaðra. Cf. Blatherskite.]
Blat`ter*a"tion, n. Etym: [L. blateratio a babbling.]
Blay, n. Etym: [AS. bl, fr. bl, bleak, white; akin to Icel. bleikja, OHG. bleicha, G. bleihe. See Bleak, n. & a.] (Zoöl.)
Blaze, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blazed; p. pr. & vb. n. Blazing.]
Bla"zon, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blazoned; p. pr. & vb. n. Blazoning.] Etym: [From blazon, n.; confused with 4th blaze: cf. F. blasonner.]
Bleak, n. Etym: [From Bleak, a., cf. Blay.] (Zoöl.)
Bleat, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bleated; p. pr. & vb. n. Bleating.] Etym: [OE. bleten, AS. bl; akin to D. blaten, bleeten, OHG. blazan, plazan; prob. of imitative origin.]
Bleed, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bled; p. pr. & vb. n. Bleeding.] Etym: [OE. bleden, AS. bl, fr. bl blood; akin to Sw. blöda, Dan. blöde, D. bloeden, G. bluten. See Blood.]

Blend, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blended or Blent; p. pr. & vb. n. Blending.] Etym: [OE. blenden, blanden, AS. blandan to blend, mix; akin to Goth. blandan to mix, Icel. blanda, Sw. blanda, Dan. blande, OHG. blantan to mis; to unknown origin.]
Blent, imp. & p. p. of Blend to mingle.
Bless"ing, n. Etym: [AS. bletsung. See Bless, v. t.]
Blet, n. Etym: [F. blet, blette, a., soft from over ripeness.]
Blind, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blinded; p. pr. & vb. n. Blinding.]
Blind"fold`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blindfolded; p. pr. & vb. n. Blindfolding.] Etym: [OE. blindfolden, blindfelden, blindfellen; AS. blind blind + prob. fellan, fyllan, to fell, strike down.]
Blind"man's buff" (. Etym: [See Buff a buffet.]
Blis"ter, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blistered; p. pr. & vb. n. Blistering.]
Blithe, a. Etym: [AS. bli blithe, kind; akin to Goth. blei kind, Icel. bli mild, gentle, Dan. & Sw. blid gentle, D. blijd blithe, OHG. blidi kind, blithe.]
Blive, adv. Etym: [A contraction of Belive.]
Block, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blocked; p. pr. & vb. n. Blocking.] Etym: [Cf. F. bloquer, fr. bloc block. See Block, n.]
Block*ade", n. Etym: [Cf. It. bloccata. See Block, v. t. ]
Block"house` (, n. Etym: [Block + house: cf. G. blockhaus.]
Bloe"dite, n. Etym: [From the chemist Blöde.] (Min.)
Blond, Blonde, a. Etym: [F., fair, light, of uncertain origin; cf. AS. blonden-feax gray-haired, old, prop. blended-haired, as a mixture of white and brown or black. See Blend, v. t. ]
Blood, n. Etym: [OE. blod, blood, AS. bl; akin to D. bloed, OHG. bluot, G. blut, Goth, bl, Sw. & Dan. blod; prob. fr. the same root as E. blow to bloom. See Blow to bloom.]
Blood"-bol`tered, a. Etym: [Blood + Prov. E. bolter to mat in tufts. Cf. Balter.]
Blood"flow`er, n. Etym: [From the color of the flower.] (Bot.)
Blood"let` (, v. t. Etym: [AS. bl; bl blood + l to let.]
Blood"shot` (, a. Etym: [Blood + shot, p. p. of shoot to variegate.]
Blood"stroke` (, n. Etym: [Cf. F. coup de sang.]
Bloom, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bloomed; p. pr. & vb. n. Blooming.]
Blos"som, n. Etym: [OE. blosme, blostme, AS. bl, bl, blossom; akin to D. bloesem, L. fios, and E. flower; from the root of E. blow to blossom. See Blow to blossom, and cf. Bloom a blossom.]
Blot, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blotted; p. pr. & vb. n. Blotting.] Etym: [Cf. Dan. plette. See 3d Blot.]
Blote, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bloted; p. pr. & vb. n. Bloting.] Etym: [Cf. Sw. blöt-fisk soaked fish, fr. blöta to soak. See 1st Bloat.]
Blouse, n. Etym: [F. blouse. Of unknown origin.]
Blowth, n. Etym: [From Blow to blossom: cf. Growth.]
Blowze, n. Etym: [Prob. from the same root as blush.]
Blub, v. t. & i. Etym: [Cf. Bleb, Blob.]
Blub"ber, n. Etym: [See Blobber, Blob, Bleb.]
Blue, a. [Compar. Bluer; superl. Bluest.] Etym: [OE. bla, blo, blew, blue, Sw. bl, D. blauw, OHG. bl, G. blau; but influenced in form by F. bleu, from OHG. blao.]
Blu"ets, n. Etym: [F. bluet, bleuet, dim. of bleu blue. See Blue, a.] (Bot.)
Blun"der, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blundered; p. pr. & vb. n. Blundering.] Etym: [OE. blunderen, blondren, to stir, confuse, blunder; perh. allied to blend to mix, to confound by mixture.]
Blunt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blunted; p. pr. & vb. n. Blunting.]
Blur, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blurred; p. pr. & vb. n. Blurring.] Etym: [Prob. of same origin as blear. See Blear.]
Blurt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Blurted; p. pr. & vb. n. Blurting.] Etym: [Cf. Blare.]

Blush v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blushed; p. pr. & vb. n. Blushing.] Etym: [OE. bluschen to shine, look, turn red, AS. blyscan to glow; akin to blysa a torch, abl to blush, D. blozen, Dan. blusse to blaze, blush.]
Blus"ter, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Blustered; p. pr. & vb. n. Blustering.] Etym: [Allied to blast.]
Bo"a con*strict"or. Etym: [NL. See Boa, and Constrictor.] (Zoöl.)
Bo`a*ner"ges. Etym: [Gr. , fr. Heb. bn sons of thunder. — an appellation given by Christ to two of his disciples (James and John). See Mark iii. 17.]
Boar, n. Etym: [OE. bar, bor, bore, AS. bar; akin to OHG. p, MHG. b, G. bär, boar (but not bär bear), and perh. Russ. borov' boar.] (Zoöl.)
Board, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Boarding.]
Boat, n. Etym: [OE. boot, bat, AS. bat; akin to Icel. batr, Sw. båt, Dan. baad, D.& G. boot. Cf. Bateau.]
Bo*a"tion, n. Etym: [L. boatus, fr. boare to roar.]
Boce, n. Etym: [L. box, bocis, Gr. , .] (Zoöl.)
Bo*dock", n. Etym: [Corrupt. fr. bois d'arc.]
Bod"rage, n. Etym: [Prob. of Celtic origin: cf. Bordrage.]
Bod"y, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bodied (p. pr. & vb. n. Bodying.]
Boer, n. Etym: [D., a farmer. See Boor.]
Bog, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bogged; p. pr. & vb. n. Bogging.]
Bog"gle, v. i. [imp & p. p. Boggled; p. pr. & vb. n. Boggling.] Etym: [ See Bogle, n.]
Bo"gie, n. [A dialectic word. N. of Eng. & Scot.]
Bo"gy, n.; pl. Bogies. Etym: [See Bogle.]

Boil, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boiled; p. pr. & vb. n. Boiling.] Etym: [OE. boilen, OF. boilir, builir, F. bouillir, fr. L. bullire to be in a bubbling motion, from bulla bubble; akin to Gr. , Lith. bumbuls. Cf. Bull an edict, Budge, v., and Ebullition.]
Boist, n. Etym: [OF. boiste, F. boîte, from the same root as E. box.]
Bo*ja"nus or"gan. Etym: [From Bojanus, the discoverer.] (Zoöl.)
Bold, a. Etym: [OE. bald, bold, AS. bald, beald; akin to Icel. ballr, OHG. bald, MHG. balt, D. boud, Goth. bal boldness, It. baldo. In Ger. there remains only bald, adv. soon. Cf. Bawd, n.]
Bold"en, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boldened. ]
Bo"lis, n. Etym: [L., fr. Gr. missile, arrow, fr. to throw.]
Boll, n. Etym: [OE. bolle boll, bowl, AS. bolla. See Bowl a vessel.]
Bol"lard, n. Etym: [Cf. Bole the stem of a tree, and Pollard.]
Boll"ing, n. Etym: [Cf. Bole stem of a tree, and Poll, v. t.]
Boln, v. i. Etym: [OE. bolnen, bollen; cf. Dan. bulne. Cf. Bulge.]
Bo*lom"e*ter, n. Etym: [Gr. a stroke, ray + -meter.] (Physics)
Bol"sa, n. [Sp., lit., purse. See Bourse.]
Bol"ster, n. Etym: [AS. bolster; akin to Icel. b, Sw. & Dan. bolster, OHG. bolstar, polstar, G. polster; from the same root as E. bole stem, bowl hollow vessel. Cf. Bulge, Poltroon.]
Bolt, n. Etym: [AS. bolt; akin to Icel. bolti, Dan. bolt, D. bout, OHG. bolz, G. bolz, bolzen; of uncertain origin.]
Bolt"sprit` (, n. Etym: [A corruption of bowsprit.] (Naut.)
Bom"bard, n. Etym: [F. bombarde, LL. bombarda, fr. L. bombus + -ard. Cf. Bumper, and see Bomb.]
Bom"bast, n. Etym: [OF. bombace cotton, LL. bombax cotton, bombasium a doublet of cotton; hence, padding, wadding, fustian. See Bombazine.]
Bom"bax, n. Etym: [LL., cotton. See Bombast, n.] (Bot.)
Bom"bic, a. Etym: [L. bombyx silk, silkworm: cf. F. bombique.]
Bom"bo*lo, n.; pl. Bomboloes. Etym: [Cf. It bombola a pitcher.]
Bom*byc"i*nous, a. Etym: [L. bombycinus. See Bombazine.]
Bom*byl"i*ous, a. Etym: [L. bombylius a bumblebee, Gr. .]
Bom"byx, n. Etym: [L., silkworm. See Bombazine.] (Zoöl.)
Bon, a. Etym: [F., fr. L. bonus.]
Bo*nan"za, n. Etym: [Sp., prop. calm., fair weather, prosperity, fr. L. bonus good.]
Bo*na"sus, Bo*nas"sus, n. Etym: [L. bonasus, Gr. , .] (Zoöl.)
Bond, n. Etym: [The same word as band. Cf. Band, Bend.]
Bond"age, n. Etym: [LL. bondagium. See Bond, a.]
Bond"man, n.; pl. Bondmen. Etym: [Bond,a.orn.+ man.]
Bonds"man, n.; pl. Bondsmen . Etym: [Bond,a.orn.+ man.]
Bon"duc, n. Etym: [F. bonduc, fr. Ar. bunduq hazel nut, filbert nut.] (Bot.)
Bond"wom`an, n.; pl. Bondwomen. Etym: [Bond,a.orn.+ woman.]
Bone, n. Etym: [OE. bon, ban, AS. ban; akin to Icel. bein, Sw. ben, Dan. & D. been, G. bein bone, leg; cf. Icel. beinn straight.]
Bon"grace` (, n. Etym: [F. bon good + grâce grace, charm.]
Bon"i*fy, v. t. Etym: [L. bonus good + -fy: cf. F. bonifier.]
Bon"ing, n. Etym: [Senses 1 and 2 fr. 1st Bone, sense 3 fr. 3d Bone.]
Bon"mot`, n.; pl. Bonsmots. Etym: [ F. bon good + mot word.]
Bon"ni*bel, n. Etym: [F. bonne et belle, good and beautiful. Cf. Bellibone.]
Bon"ny, a. [Spelled bonnie by the Scotch.] Etym: [OE. boni, prob. fr. F. bon, fem. bonne, good, fr. L. bonus good. See Bounty, and cf. Bonus, Boon.]
Bon"spiel, n. Etym: [Scot.; of uncertain origin.]
Bon" ton". Etym: [F., good tone, manner.]
Bo"nus, n.; pl. Bonuses (. Etym: [L. bonus good. Cf. Bonny.]
Boo`hoe", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boohooed; p. pr. & vb. n. Boohooing.] Etym: [An imitative word.]
Book"land`, Bock"land`, n. Etym: [AS. b; b book + land land.] (O. Eng. Law)
Boom (boom), n. Etym: [D. boom tree, pole, beam, bar. See Beam.]
Boom"das, n. Etym: [D. boom tree + das badger.] (Zoöl.)
Boom"slang*e, n. Etym: [D. boom tree + slang snake.] (Zoöl.)
Boon, a. Etym: [F. bon. See Boon, n.]
Boor, n. Etym: [D. boer farmer, boor; akin to AS. geb countryman, G. bauer; fr. the root of AS. b to inhabit, and akin to E. bower, be. Cf. Neighbor, Boer, and Big to build.]
Boost, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boosted; p. pr. & vb. n. Boosting.] Etym: [Cf. Boast, v. i.]
Boot, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Booted; p. pr. & vb. n. Booting.]
Bo*ö"tes, n. Etym: [L. Bootes, Gr. herdsman, fr. , gen. , ox, cow.] (Astron.)
Boot"hale`, v. t. & i. Etym: [Boot, for booty + hale.]
Boot"tree`, n. Etym: [Boot + tree wood, timber.]
Booze, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Boozed; p. pr. & vb. n. Boozing.] Etym: [D. buizen; akin to G. bausen, and perh. fr. D. buis tube, channel, bus box, jar.]
Bo*rac"ic, a. Etym: [Cf. F. boracique. See Borax.]
Bo"rax, n. Etym: [OE. boras, fr. F. borax, earlier spelt borras; cf. LL. borax, Sp. borraj; all fr. Ar. b, fr. Pers. b.]
Bor"del, Bor*del"lo, n. Etym: [F. bordel, orig. a little hut, OF. borde hut, cabin, of German origin, and akin to E. board,n.See. Board, n.]
Bor"der, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bordered; p. pr. & vb. n. Bordering.]
Bord"land`, n. Etym: [Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + land.] (O. Eng. Law)
Bord"lode`, n. Etym: [Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + lode leading.] (O. Eng. Law)
Bord"man, n. Etym: [Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + man.]
Bord" serv`ice. Etym: [Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + service.] (O. Eng. Law)
Bor"dure, n. Etym: [F. bordure. See Border, n.] (Her.)
Bo"re*al, a. Etym: [L. borealis: cf. F. boréal. See Boreas.]
Bore"cole`, n. Etym: [Cf. D. boerenkool (lit.) husbandman's cabbage.]
Born, p. p. & a. Etym: [See Bear, v. t.]
Bor"nite, n. Etym: [Named after Von Born, a mineralogist.] (Min.)
Bor"rel, a. Etym: [Prob. from Borrel, n.]

Bosh"vark, n. Etym: [D. bosch wood + varken pig.] (Zoöl.)
Boss, n.; pl. Bosses. Etym: [OE. boce, bose, boche, OF. boce, boche, bosse, F. bosse, of G. origin; cf. OHG. bozo tuft, bunch, OHG. bozan, MHG. bôzen, to beat. See Beat, and cf. Botch a swelling.]

Bos"set, n. Etym: [Cf. Boss a stud.] (Zoöl.)
Bos"tryx, n. [NL.; irreg. fr. Gr. a curl.] (Bot.)
Bo*tan"ic, Bo*tan"ic*al, a. Etym: [Cf. F. botanique. See Botany.]
Bot"a*nize, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Botanized; p. pr. & vb. n. Botanizing.] Etym: [Cf. F. botaniser.]

Bot"a*no*man`cy, n. Etym: [Botany + -mancy: cf. F. botanomantie.]

Bot"tom*ry, n. Etym: [From 1st Bottom in sense 8: cf.D. bodemerij. Cf. Bummery.] (Mar.Law)
Bou`chées", n. pl. Etym: [F., morsels, mouthfuls, fr. bouche mouth.] (Cookery)
Bou*doir", n. [F., fr. bouder to pout, be sulky.]
Bouge, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bouged] Etym: [Variant of bulge. Cf. Bowge.]
Bou"get, n. Etym: [Cf. F. bougette sack, bag. Cf. Budget.] (Her.)
Bought, n. Etym: [Cf. Dan. bugt bend, turning, Icel. bug. Cf. Bight, Bout, and see Bow to bend.]
Bou*gie" (, n. Etym: [F. bougie wax candle, bougie, fr. Bougie, Bugia, a town of North Africa, from which these candles were first imported into Europe.]
Bou`illi" (, n. Etym: [F., fr. bouillir to boil.] (Cookery)
Bou`illon" (, n. Etym: [F., fr. bouillir to boil.]
Bouk, n. Etym: [AS. bücbauch, Icel. bü body.]
Bou*lan"ger*ite, n. Etym: [From Boulanger, a French mineralogist.] (Min.)
Bou"le*vard`, n. Etym: [F. boulevard, boulevart, fr. G. bollwerk. See Bulwark.]
Boule`verse`ment", n. Etym: [F., fr. bouleverser to overthrow.]
Bounce, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Bounced; p. pr. & vb. n. Bouncing.] Etym: [OE. bunsen; cf. D. bonzen to strike, bounce, bons blow, LG. bunsen to knock; all prob. of imitative origin.]
Bound, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Bounding.]
Bound"en, p.p & a. Etym: [Old. p. p. of bind.]
Boun"te*ous, a. Etym: [OE. bountevous, fr. bounte bounty.]

Bourd, n. Etym: [F. bourde fib, lie, OF. borde, bourde, jest, joke.]

Bo"vi*form, a. Etym: [L. bos, bovis, ox + -form.]
Bowd"ler*ize, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bowdlerized; p. pr. & vb. n. Bowdlerizing.] [After Dr. Thomas Bowdler, an English physician, who published an expurgated edition of Shakespeare in 1818.]
Bow"el, n. Etym: [OE. bouel, bouele, OF. boel, boele, F. boyau, fr. L. botellus a small sausage, in LL. also intestine, dim. of L. botulus sausage.]
Bow"en*ite, n. Etym: [From G.T.Bowen, who analyzed it in 1822.] (Min.)
Bo"wer, n. Etym: [From Bow, v. & n.]
Bowl, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bowled; p. pr. & vb. n. Bowling.]

Bowse, v. i. Etym: [See Booze, and Bouse.]
Bow"yer, n. Etym: [From Bow, like lawyer from law.]
Box, n. Etym: [As. box, L. buxus, fr. Gr. Box a case.] (Bot.)
Box"haul`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Boxhauled.] (Naut.)

Brach*el"y*tra, n. pl. Etym: [NL., fr. Gr. ( (Zoöl.)
Brach"man, n. Etym: [L. Brachmanae, pl., Gr.

Brac"te*ole, n. Etym: [L. bracteola, dim. of bractea. See Bractea.] (Bot.)
Brae, n. Etym: [See Bray a hill.]
Brag`ga*do"cio, n. Etym: [From Braggadocchio, a boastful character in Spenser's "Faërie Queene."]

Brah"man, Brah"min, n.; pl. Brahmans, Brahmins. Etym: [Skr. Brahmana (cf. Brahman worship, holiness; the God Brahma, also Brahman): cf. F. Brahmane, Brachmane, Bramine, L. Brachmanae, -manes, -mani, pl., Gr.
Brain, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Brained; p. pr. & vb. n. Braining.]

Bram"bling, n. Etym: [OE. bramline. See Bramble, n.] (Zoöl.)
Bran, n. Etym: [OE. bren, bran, OF. bren, F. bran, from Celtic; cf. Armor. brenn, Ir. bran, bran, chaff.]
Bran"chi*a, n.; pl. Branchiæ. Etym: [L., fr. Gr. (Anat.)

Bran"chi*u"ra, n. pl. Etym: [NL., fr., Gr. (Zoöl.)
Brand, v.t [imp. & p. p. Branded; p. pr. & vb. n. Branding.].

Bran"dish, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Brandished; p. pr. & vb. n. Brandishing.] Etym: [OE. braundisen, F. brandir, fr. brand a sword, fr. OHG. brant brand. See Brand, n.]

Bran"gle, v.i [imp. & p. p. Brangled; p. pr. & vb. n. Brangling.]

Bran"sle, n. Etym: [See Brawl a dance.]

Brast, v. t. & i. Etym: [See Burst.]

Brat, n. Etym: [OE. bratt coarse garnment, AS. bratt cloak, fr. the Celtic; cf. W. brat clout, rag, Gael. brat cloak, apron, raf, Ir. brat cloak; properly then, a child's bib or clout; hence, a child.]
Brave, a. [Compar. Braver; superl. Bravest.] Etym: [F. brave, It. or Sp. bravo, (orig.) fierce, wild, savage, prob. from. L. barbarus. See Barbarous, and cf. Bravo.]

Braw, a. [See Brave, a.] [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]
Bray, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Brayed; p. pr. & vb. n. Braying.] Etym: [OE. brayen, OF. breier, F. broyer to pound, grind, fr. OHG. brehhan to break. See Break.]

Braz"i*lin, n. Etym: [Cf. F. brésiline. See Brazil.] (Chem.)

Braze, Brasier); or Ar. vars plant for dyeing red or yellow. This name was given to the wood from its color; and it is said that King Emanuel, of Portugal, gave the name Brazil to the country in South America on account of its producing this wood.]
Breach, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Breached ( ; p. pr. & vb. n. Breaching.]

Breathe, v. i. [imp. & p. p Breathed; p. pr. & vb. n. Breathing.] Etym: [From Breath.]

Breech"es, n. pl. Etym: [OE. brech, brek, AS. brek, pl. of broc breech, breeches; akin to Icel. brok breeches, ODan. brog, D. broek, G. bruch; cf. L. bracae, braccae, which is of Celtic origin. Cf. Brail.]

Breed, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bred; p. pr. & vb. n. Breeding.] Etym: [OE. breden, AS. bredan to nourish, cherish, keep warm, from brod brood; akin to D. broeden to brood, OHG. bruoten, G. brüten. See Brood.]
Breeze, n. Etym: [F. braise cinders, live coals. See Brasier.]

Bren, Bren"ne, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Brent (p. pr. & vb. n. Brenning.] Etym: [See Burn.]

Bres"te, v. t. & i. [imp. Brast; p. p. Brusten, Borsten, Bursten.]

Brews"ter*ite, n. Etym: [Named after Sir David Brewster.]

Bride"groom`, n. Etym: [OE. bridegome, brudgume, AS. br (akin to OS. br, D. bruidegom, bruigom, OHG. pr, MHG. briutegome, G. bräutigam); AS. br bride + guma man, akin to Goth. guma, Icel. gumi, OHG. gomo, L. homo; the insertion of r being caused by confusion with groom. See Bride, and cf. Groom, Homage.]
Bridge, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bridged (; p. pr. & vb. n. Bridging.]

Bri"dle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Bridled; p. pr. & vb. n. Bridling.]
Bri*doon", n. Etym: [F. bridon, from bride; of German origin. See Bridle, n.] (Mil.)
Bri*gade", n. Etym: [F. brigade, fr. It. brigata troop, crew, brigade, originally, a contending troop, fr. briga trouble, quarrel. See Brigand.]
Brig`a*dier" gen"er*al. Etym: [F. brigadier, fr. brigade.] (Mil.)
Bright"en, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Brightened; p. pr. & vb. n. Brightening.]

Bril*lan"te, adv. Etym: [It. See Brilliant, a.] (Mus.)

Brim, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Brimmed; p. pr. & vb. n. Brimming.]

Bring, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Brought; p. pr. & vb. n. Bringing.] Etym: [OE. bringen, AS. bringan; akin to OS. brengian, D. brengen, Fries. brenga, OHG. bringan, G. bringen, Goth. briggan.]
Bri*quette", n. [Also briquet.] [F., dim. of brique brick.]
Brisk, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Bricked; p. pr. & vb. n. Bricking.]

Bro*cade", n. Etym: [Sp. brocado (cf. It. broccato, F. brocart), fr. LL. brocare *prick, to figure (textile fabrics), to emboss (linen), to stitch. See Broach.]
Bro`chette" (bro`shet"), n. [F., dim. of broche. See Broach, n.] (Cookery)
Bro*chure", n. Etym: [F., fr. brocher to stitch. See Broach, v. t.]

Brock"en spec"ter or Brock"en spec"tre. [Trans. of G. Brockengespenst.]
